content: Programs have the flexibility to collect additional information based on local needs and context. A standardized list of key terminology and definitions is provided to ensure accurate patient monitoring and measurement of program indicators. This harmonized approach facilitates consistency in data collection and reporting both within and across countries. The updated WHO minimum dataset for HIV enrollment includes several changes: Universal ART initiation has replaced previously recommended eligibility criteria. Enrollment status now reflects differentiated care models. Categories for prior ARV use have been updated to include pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Patient residence district is now recorded. Family status information has been updated. The date of the first HIV-positive test is included as a prompt for action. Relevant chronic conditions (formerly referred to as relevant medical conditions) have been updated. Concomitant medications are now documented. For ART data: The status at the start of ART has been revised. Newly recommended ARV regimens and codes for adults, pregnant and breastfeeding women, adolescents, and children have been updated. Information on switching to or substituting within third-line regimens (including regimen, date, and reason) has been added. Updates have been made to ART treatment-limiting toxicities and adverse drug reactions. Reasons for non-adherence, ARV drug substitutions, and stopping ART have been revised. Follow-up status codes and definitions have been updated. Clinical staging is no longer required for routine monitoring, as it is no longer necessary to determine treatment eligibility under the new ARV treatment guidelines. However, clinical staging may still be useful at enrollment to guide differentiated care in the absence of CD4 count, particularly for patients with advanced disease. Key terms and definitions used in this guidance include: HIV care: Routine clinical assessment, monitoring, and management, including ART, tailored to the patient’s needs. Newly enrolled in HIV care: Refers to individuals with a confirmed HIV diagnosis who present to a facility for the first time, where an HIV care record is initiated. WHO recommends prompt ART initiation for all individuals living with HIV, regardless of CD4 count. Retention in HIV care: Refers to patients who are alive and actively receiving routine HIV care, including ART, at a specific time point after enrollment or ART initiation. Retention is a critical measure of treatment success and excludes those who have died, been lost to follow-up, or transferred out. Lost to follow-up (LTF): Patients who have not been seen at the clinic for at least 90 days after their last missed appointment. Facilities are encouraged to contact patients as soon as they miss an appointment rather than waiting for the 90-day period. Transfer in (TI): Patients who transfer from one facility to another within the same system, with records or knowledge of their ART regimen and start date. These patients are classified as Transfer In and are entered into the ART register under their original ART start group. Transfer out (TO): Refers to the date a patient transfers out of a facility to continue care elsewhere. Dead: Refers to patients who die at any time after enrollment in HIV care. Substitute: Refers to the replacement of ARV drugs within the same line of treatment (e.g., first-line, second-line, or third-line regimens), with documentation of the date and reason. Switch: Refers to a change from one line of treatment to another (e.g., first-line to second-line), with documentation of the date and reason. Cumulative ever started on ART: The total number of patients who have ever started ART as new patients at a specific facility. This includes those currently on ART and those who have stopped ART but remain in care. The HIV patient monitoring system is designed to track individuals with confirmed HIV diagnoses through the continuum of care, from enrollment and ART initiation to sustained viral suppression. Health-care workers are responsible for assigning unique patient IDs, recording clinical information, and ensuring continuity of care across facilities. This system supports comprehensive monitoring and reporting to improve patient outcomes and program effectiveness.
